Now, even opponents of the issue ask very specific, targeted questions about public health, labeling, packaging requirements — you're not getting laughed out of the office anymore, and that in itself is a measure of success. Not a lot is getting passed on Capitol Hill generally right now, cannabis or otherwise, so the quantifiable metrics look different than in other industries. But in the last five years, we've passed safe banking out of the House seven times, the Senate Majority Leader has introduced a cannabis legalization bill, we're having meaningful policy discussions about appropriations provisions, and we're sitting a week after the comment period closed on the first-ever move to reclassify cannabis under the Controlled Substances Act — those are all real metrics of winning and momentum. At the state level it's more quantifiable — another state added to the medical or adult-use list. At the federal level, it's about keeping the conversation top of mind and shifting it in a way that ultimately leads to passage through both chambers and something reaching the president's desk.

Erin Moffet: For government time, especially DC time, we're moving fast, even if not as fast as people predicted after President Obama's administration, which people expected the next administration to build on. Instead we had arguably the most unfriendly cannabis attorney general in US history, which put things on pause, and then COVID put everything on pause again. So we're picking back up now. To David's point on momentum, it's every time someone who voted yes last Congress puts their name on the bill again, every time someone who previously said no takes a meeting, every time staff show up to an educational event they hadn't engaged with before. Our executive director, Saphira Galoob, said something recently that's really important to remember — that this rescheduling momentum is not the end but the beginning of this movement. We're finally at the point where cannabis policy reform is happening, but the first real step hasn't been taken yet. Everything we've done over eleven years of safe banking efforts, and since 1996 with states legalizing medical cannabis, was all Olympic qualifying — now it's game time, and what we do moving forward is what will shape US cannabis policy ten years from now.

Bryan Fields: What do you think are the most important conversations that need to happen over the next six months to keep this momentum going, especially with the election?

David Mangone: It's recognizing that this is an issue that wins with voters time after time — on the state level, ballot initiatives outperform Senate and House candidates of both parties. It's something voters are engaged on and interested in, and if I were an elected official, I'd want to be on the right side of it, given the polling support — Democrats typically higher, but a majority of both parties support full legalization, and medical support runs upward of seventy-five percent, even among traditional primary voters of both parties. That's an issue I could run on with seventy-five percent-plus popularity and not take advantage of it would be a mistake. Pew reported earlier this year that about seventy-seven percent of Americans live in a county with a regulated dispensary, so even if you're not personally participating in an adult-use or medical marketplace, you know someone who is, and perceptions have changed. Oklahoma, for example, is a state where every county voted for Donald Trump in 2016, and they passed a medical initiative by almost ten points — this is no longer purely a red-state or blue-state issue. There will always be a subset of members opposed for personal reasons — family history with addiction, religious reasons, particularly on the Evangelical right — but for most people, they simply haven't formed an opinion because they haven't had to. With thirty-eight medical states now, and likely twenty-five or more adult-use states after this election, it's become an issue politicians can't ignore. My hope for the next six months is that those who haven't gotten on the train get on it, and those already on board put it full speed ahead.

Erin Moffet: I'd focus less on the election and more on what happens in the six months after the comment period closes on this historic rescheduling — how it shakes out, what the timing looks like, what else the administration must do. Moving cannabis in the CSA has limited impact on its own; it doesn't fix everything. We still need safe banking — rescheduling doesn't provide banking access. We still desperately need criminal justice reform — cannabis crimes were written into the code out of animus, and moving from Schedule I to Schedule III doesn't even change how most people are charged. It doesn't address regulatory structure or how we maintain a safe, regulated market — we've seen the chaos that resulted from how hemp was legalized in the Farm Bill and the public health damage unregulated products can cause. None of that gets fixed by rescheduling alone, because rescheduling is just about how DEA and FDA handle a drug's classification. There's a great bipartisan bill from Congressman Dave Joyce called the PREPARE Act, which prepares agencies now for that inevitable moment — whether cannabis becomes federally legal or descheduled — so that when it happens, it's done thoughtfully rather than with ideas thrown at the wall without understanding real impacts. It should defer to the leadership already shown by the states while ensuring baseline safety standards for consumers, whether for medical or adult use, and ensuring fairness for the industry — there are things foreign cannabis companies can access in the US that domestic cannabis companies still can't. In the next six months, regardless of the election outcome, there are things this administration can still do before President Biden leaves office, and whoever comes next can build on that — but it's well beyond time for Congress to pass safe banking before the end of the year and put in place things like the PREPARE Act so we're better prepared for this inevitable transition.

Bryan Fields: I love it. I can't imagine how difficult your jobs are — I could ask you questions for ten hours trying to understand all the nuance, and I know some questions just don't have easy answers. I appreciate you both taking the time. Thank you for all you do, and I'm looking forward to having you back when we get some eventual progress.

David Mangone: Sounds great, happy to come back.

Bryan Fields: Thanks so much, thanks guys.
summary: This episode of The Dime features David Mangone and Erin of The Liaison Group, federal cannabis lobbyists representing the National Cannabis Roundtable, explaining how cannabis lobbying actually works — from building trust with congressional offices to using data, polling, and trusted messengers to move policy forward. They break down real-world strategy around safe banking, the Farm Bill, and cannabis rescheduling, including why relationship-building and education matter more than hard asks, and why rescheduling alone won't fix banking, taxation, or criminal justice issues facing the industry. It's a useful listen for anyone wanting to understand the mechanics of federal cannabis advocacy and what still needs to happen after rescheduling.
takeaways: Cannabis lobbying is primarily about education, not hard selling — staffers and members need continuous, data-backed context because cannabis touches nearly every policy area (health, banking, veterans, criminal justice).
Effective lobbying requires building long-term trust with congressional offices before ever making an ask; approaching cold with a request is usually ineffective.
Finding the right messenger matters — a well-liked, credible member like Rep. Dave Joyce (R-OH) can move colleagues who wouldn't otherwise engage on cannabis policy.

Organizations like the National Cannabis Roundtable are consensus-driven, meaning their policy positions have buy-in from small operators up through large MSOs, which strengthens credibility on the Hill.
Timing and targeting are critical — lobbyists tailor messaging to a staffer's specific committee assignment and avoid overwhelming offices with irrelevant issues.

Rescheduling cannabis to Schedule III would remove the 280E tax burden and enable more research, but it would not fix banking access, criminal justice issues, or create a federal regulatory framework.

Momentum in federal cannabis policy is measured differently than typical legislative wins — repeated House passage of SAFE Banking, growing co-sponsorships, and the 2024 rescheduling comment period are all seen as signs of progress.
Bills like the bipartisan PREPARE Act aim to get federal agencies ready for eventual descheduling or broader legalization so the transition is orderly rather than reactive.

faq.question: What does cannabis lobbying actually involve, according to The Liaison Group?
faq.answer: It's a coordinated, ongoing effort to educate lawmakers and their staff — explaining why a policy change is needed and how it affects their district — rather than simply pushing for a vote. Trust-building and providing reliable data are central to the process.

faq.question: Why is cannabis considered a uniquely complex issue to lobby on?
faq.answer: Because it's a nascent industry that touches nearly every policy area — healthcare, banking, veterans affairs, criminal justice, taxation — so there's no single committee or clear precedent, and there's still a significant education gap among lawmakers.

faq.question: How do lobbyists decide which members of Congress to prioritize?
faq.answer: They track factors like committee assignments, home state cannabis laws, prior voting history, and whether a member has a high veteran population or personal connection to the issue, focusing energy on those most likely to be persuadable or influential.

faq.question: Would moving cannabis to Schedule III fix the industry's biggest problems?
faq.answer: No. Rescheduling would remove the 280E tax burden and enable more research, but it would not create federal banking access, address criminal justice reform, or establish a federal regulatory framework for the existing state markets.

faq.question: What is the PREPARE Act and why does it matter?
faq.answer: It's a bipartisan bill from Rep. Dave Joyce designed to get federal agencies proactively planning for the eventual rescheduling or descheduling of cannabis, so that regulatory changes are thoughtful rather than reactive when that day comes.

faq.question: How do lobbyists handle competing information from opposition groups?
faq.answer: By sourcing all claims directly from government data — state regulators, the DEA, HHS — and citing sources transparently, rather than relying on unverifiable talking points, while focusing persuasion efforts on persuadable audiences rather than entrenched opponents.

faq.question: Why do lobbyists avoid pairing cannabis bills like SAFE Banking with unrelated legislation?
faq.answer: Because tying cannabis reform to controversial or unrelated provisions risks losing support from coalition partners (like banking or insurance associations) who may object more to the paired provision than they support cannabis reform itself.

faq.question: What signs indicate real momentum in federal cannabis policy, given how little legislation passes?
faq.answer: Repeated passage of SAFE Banking through the House, growing bipartisan co-sponsorship, serious appropriations riders debates, and the 2024 rescheduling comment period are cited as meaningful, if incremental, markers of progress.
